metadata.title: 2 dead and about 15 people may be missing as flash flood tears through the Grand Canyon

sources.text:
Hikers describe flash flood in Grand Canyon that left 2 dead, 14 others missing
A sudden flash flood in the Grand Canyon killed two people, left 14 missing, and caused significant destruction to campsites and trails.
A sudden flash flood in the Grand Canyon on Saturday killed two people, left 14 others missing, and caused extensive damage to campsites, trails and infrastructure.
The flood, caused by a monsoon storm, swept through Bright Angel Campground and Phantom Ranch, destroying bridges, campsites and buildings. Officials confirmed the body of a 46-year-old man was recovered from the Colorado River on Saturday night.
What we know about the victims
Officials identified one of the victims as Dr. John Giusti, whose body was recovered. Two of his friends, Brent Rosenkranz and Timothy Allen Smith, remain missing.
The three friends, all from Granbury, Texas, had been excited to take this vacation trip together to the Grand Canyon.
Search and rescue efforts are ongoing as authorities work to locate the missing individuals.
The missing individuals are believed to be hikers and backpackers who were on trails when the flood hit.
Witnesses describe the scene
"This one was black water, turbulent water, moving very quickly," hiker David Gregory said. "It sounded like little thunder as they were kind of crashing onto each other."
Gregory and his friend's family were ordered to evacuate and run across a footbridge to higher ground.
"If they hadn't told us to evacuate when they did, I don't think it would have been a way. A lot of people wouldn't have made it," hiker Gabe Bergemann said.
Just 10 minutes after the evacuation, the footbridge was gone. Campers described watching a wall of water tear through Phantom Ranch, sweeping away boulders, an excavator and even entire buildings.
"There was a fridge. We even saw the scariest thing was there was like a cabin that washed down the river, and we could like see the roof of the cabin and the bed from the cabin that was in the river," Bergemann said.
More than 60 people were airlifted out of the area by helicopter.
"Ranger Kate, God bless her. She's the one that orchestrated all this and saved everybody," camper Scott Svedin said. "It would have been wiped out, all of us."
The disaster also knocked out the park's only water pipeline, which serves tourists and residents, forcing lodges and hotels to close to overnight visitors.

The National Park Service is currently managing a dire situation in the Grand Canyon, where severe flash flooding has caused extensive damage to critical infrastructure and left officials searching for 15 potentially missing hikers. The flooding, which struck the Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch area, has forced the park to implement stage four water restrictions.
As reported by the NY Post, restrictions are a direct result of the storm causing extensive damage to the Transcanyon Waterline, which is the primary source of water for the park. Park officials claimed that they recovered the body of a 46-year-old man from the Colorado River on Sunday night. While the identity of this individual has not been released to the public, the search for 15 other people who are believed to be missing is currently the top priority.
The stage four water restrictions now in place are quite strict and will affect the day-to-day operations of the park. These measures reportedly include forced dry camping with no access to water spigots and the temporary closure of overnight lodgings. Additionally, there is a strict no-fire rule in effect for the South Rim and inner canyon areas to prevent any further complications.
Almost every footbridge has been destroyed
The scale of the destruction is quite significant. Nearly all of the footbridges spanning Bright Angel Creek were reportedly completely destroyed by the rushing water. The physical damage includes a historic lodge near the bottom of the site and untold environmental impact across the region. Since the flooding began on Saturday, park officials claim they have successfully evacuated at least 62 people from the area.
The National Park Service is asking anyone who knows of hikers or backpackers who were in the inner canyon along the Bright Angel Creek corridor on August 29, as well as anyone who had a campground reservation in the affected corridor, to provide information to the National Park Service Investigative Services Branch. They are relying on public tips to help narrow down the search area and find those who are still unaccounted for.
Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs stated that state emergency officials are coordinating with federal and local authorities to provide necessary support. She shared her thoughts on the situation on X, writing, “My heart is with the families and loved ones of every person unaccounted for after the flash flooding at the Grand Canyon. DEMA is coordinating with NPS and Coconino County Emergency Management to support search and recovery efforts.”
Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes also addressed the incident through a press release, describing the flash flooding as “devastating.” He expressed gratitude toward the first responders who are working tirelessly to search for those still missing and assisting with the evacuation of others from the affected areas.
Published: Aug 31, 2026 04:30 pm

Two dead, two missing in Grand Canyon flash flooding
Family members have identified a hiker killed in weekend flooding in the Grand Canyon as a Texas chiropractor and say two other men who went on their dream trip remain missing.
John Giusti and his friends planned to spend two nights at the bottom of the canyon fishing and exploring. They spoke to their families on Thursday and found their campsite on Friday. They have not been heard from since, the three families said in a joint statement released on Monday.
Searchers on the air and ground continue to look for Brent Rosenkranz and Timothy Smith, their families said.
Rescue crews looking for missing people have found at least two bodies since a major flash flood swept through the Grand Canyon, and forecasters warned on Monday that more flooding was possible as heavy rain shrouded the canyon walls.
More than a dozen people were missing following waves of rain in the Bright Angel Creek area of Grand Canyon National Park, which hosts 4.4 million visitors a year.
Saturday's flash flood severely damaged the only water pipeline into the canyon.
Officials barred tourists from staying at lodges and hotels inside Grand Canyon National Park and issued emergency water restrictions for year-round residents.
The flood threatened people who hike far into the Grand Canyon
The flood happened deep in the canyon near where the Colorado River flows, around popular lodges and camping areas where people hiking from one rim of the Grand Canyon to the other stop for the night.
Scores of visitors had to be evacuated from the area by helicopter. They talked of a massive deluge and rangers warning of rockslides, and saw huge pools of logs and debris rolling down the river as they stood nearby awaiting rescue.
Hiker Daniel Evans said it rained several times before the worst 30-minute downpour on Saturday afternoon. He had been planning to rest through the hot day and spend the night near the hard-hit Bright Angel campground area.
Earlier, rangers told him it looked to be safe. Then, as the rain poured, they told him it was time to go. He thought of Nepal and the massive floods and landslides that poured down mountain valleys last week.
"The entire time it was raining - the entire time I'm going through all this and packing - I'm just keeping my eyes upstream, just praying that a wall of water isn't coming toward us," Evans said.
The body of a 46-year-old man was recovered on Sunday evening near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River, the National Park Service said without providing details. Crews on Monday were trying to recover a second body, park officials said in an email that provided no other details.
More than a dozen people remained missing and officials urged anyone who was in the park when the flood happened to contact park rangers or anyone else to let them know they are okay.
Late on Monday morning more rain fell as the state Department of Emergency and Military Affairs was co-ordinating with the park service and county emergency management officials in search and recovery efforts.

CBS News
Two deaths have been confirmed and some 15 people were believed to be missing Monday morning in Grand Canyon National Park after parts of the canyon were hit by major flash floods over the weekend. The raging waters swept boulders, infrastructure and other debris into the Colorado River after a storm dropped a huge amount of precipitation in a very short period of time, officials said.
The body of a 46-year-old man was recovered Sunday evening near Crystal Rapids on the Colorado River, the National Park Service said, without providing any additional information. On Monday, the park service said a second body had been recovered.
The NPS called for anyone who knew of hikers or backpackers who were in Bright Angel Canyon or the Phantom Ranch area on Saturday afternoon, when the flash floods hit, to provide information to park authorities.

(NEW YORK) — Rescuers are bracing for more treacherous weather at the Grand Canyon Monday as authorities confirmed another body had been recovered amid a search for 14 people who “may be missing or unaccounted” in a deadly flash flood that struck the national park over the weekend.
The National Park Service said the body was pulled from the flooded area, bringing the death toll to two.
On Sunday evening, officials said the body of a 46-year-old man was recovered near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River.
The names of the deceased have not been released.
Flood survivors told ABC News that they ran for their lives when a flood swept through the floor of the Grand Canyon on Saturday afternoon, wiping out campgrounds, structures, hiking trails and vital infrastructure, according to officials.
The National Weather Service has issued a flood watch for the Grand Canyon through at least Monday evening, warning that “flash flooding caused by excessive rainfall continues to be possible” for all of northern and central Arizona.
Air evacuations continued on Sunday afternoon, a day after a “significant flash flood” swept through campgrounds and hiking trails at the bottom of the national park, authorities said.
The Grand Canyon National Park Service said in an update Sunday evening that one person was recovered from the Colorado River in the park. The identity of the deceased individual has not been released.
NPS said there are at least 14 other individuals “who may be missing or unaccounted” following the flash flood.
“The National Park Service is asking anyone who knows of hikers or backpackers who were in the inner canyon along the Bright Angel Creek corridor on August 29, as well as anyone who had a campground reservation in the affected corridor, to provide information to the National Park Service Investigative Services Branch (ISB),” the statement said.
Earlier Sunday, the National Park Service (NPS) officials said more than 20 were missing and 62 individuals were air evacuated from Grand Canyon’s Phantom Ranch and the lower North Kaibab Trail, “which was affected by a significant flash-flood event Saturday afternoon.”
Evacuees were being taken to the Maswik Lodge Cafeteria on the South Rim of the Grand Canyon, where the American Red Cross is coordinating assistance.
No injuries were immediately reported.
The latest National Park Service said the flash flooding knocked out the park’s water pipeline, prompting “significant water conservation measures” to be implemented. Those measures include: no overnight hotel stays allowed starting Monday, and only campground bathroom faucets will still run.
“Multiple campgrounds and trails are closed until further notice, and there is no estimated reopening date for the affected areas,” the Grand Canyon NPS said.
Grand Canyon National Park staff, in coordination with the Arizona Department of Public Safety, were continuing air evacuations on Sunday afternoon, officials said.
“Grand Canyon will possibly face additional thunderstorms and heavy rainfall today and Monday, which could result in flash flooding, debris flow, and rockfall,” the Grand Canyon NPS statement said.
Flash flooding unfolded about 2:30 p.m. local time on Saturday in the Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch area, both popular destinations for hikers.
“The flash flood resulted in significant impacts to infrastructure throughout Bright Angel Canyon. Nearly all footbridges spanning Bright Angel Creek were destroyed, eliminating hiker access across the creek,” the Grand Canyon NPS said.
Saturday’s flash-flood event occurred after four rounds of rain swept across parts of the Grand Canyon over a span of about six hours, according to the National Weather Service (NWS). The initial three rounds were not very heavy, but saturated the soil and left the area much more prone to dangerous flash flooding once the fourth round of torrential rain moved through.
The steepness of the canyon and the burn scar from last year’s Dragon Bravo Fire on the North Rim were likely major contributors, the NWS said.
Videos of the flooding obtained by ABC News show a roaring Colorado River as mudflows and debris from metal structures are seen floating down the river.
Erica Viola, who recorded the videos, told ABC News she was camping at Bright Angel Campground when she and her husband, Scott Svedin, had to evacuate. Viola said that she lost most of her belongings in the flooding.
Viola said that she and other campers were told by park rangers to run as fast as they could to the nearest bridge for evacuation.
Svedin said that as they were headed for the bridge, people were scrambling to beat the rising water.
“We just heard people yell, ‘Run, run, run!’ And there’s 40 of us running through this deep, muddy water, trying to make it to the bridge,” Viola said. “Once we got to the bridge, that’s when this 15-foot wall of water came through the campground in Phantom Ranch and just wiped out all the bridges in the creek.”
Viola and Svedin said they witnessed bunkhouses, barbecue grills, ice chests, and even an excavator floating down the Colorado River.
ABC News’ Jennifer Watts, Lissette Rodriguez and Dan Peck contributed to this report.
